data.text:
Results are JSON strings.**Claim 0: Nitrifying 1 g of ammonia nitrogen into nitrate uses about 4.57 g of oxygen. Supported as written.**
- A *Water Research* paper on nitrification stoichiometry says: Theoretically, 4.57 g of oxygen are needed to completely oxidize 1 g of ammonia–nitrogen. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0043135412005623)
- A wastewater patent (US 8,287,734) says: Based on the theoretical stoichiometry for the biological nitrification process 4.57 g O2/g N is needed for complete oxidation of ammonia to nitrate. (https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/8287734)
- Both sources call it a theoretical figure. Real systems differ a little, because nitrifiers also take up some nitrogen to grow.

**Claim 1: Goldfish can remember things for at least three months, not three seconds. Supported as written.**
- Discover Wildlife says: goldfish can retain memories for at least three months, can be trained, and can also tell the time. (https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/fish/goldfish-memory)
- The American Museum of Natural History describes a student experiment. The goldfish were tested at two-, three-, four-, and six-month intervals to see whether they recalled the location of the food. (https://www.amnh.org/learn-teach/curriculum-collections/young-naturalist-awards/goldfish-as-a-model-for-understanding-learning-and-memory-more-complex-than-you-think)
- Science ABC says experiments show recall for weeks to months. (https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/animals/do-goldfish-really-have-a-3-second-memory)
- These are popular-science sources and a student project, not peer-reviewed papers. The "at least three months" wording is safe, but I would not attribute it to a single formal study without checking.

**Claim 2: Unionized ammonia at about 0.02 mg/L can start to harm fish gills. Supported in a corrected form.**
- The 0.02 mg/L figure is real, but it is usually described as a general or chronic safety threshold. It is not a specific gill-damage threshold. Sources differ on where harm starts.
- A University of Tennessee fisheries course page says: The generally accepted rule of thumb is that un-ionized ammonia in excess of 0.02 mg/L is potentially toxic. (http://web.utk.edu/~rstrange/wfs556/html-content/05-ammonia.html)
- A review by The Nature Conservancy says less than 0.020 mg/L unionized ammonia is considered safe for fish reproduction (EPA 1989). (https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/documents/literature-review-ammonia.pdf)
- A *Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia* study says: Continuous or frequent exposure to NH3 concentrations above 0.02 mg/L can cause intense irritation of the gills. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352513422003210)
- Texas A&M AgriLife Extension (a government-affiliated source) uses a higher number: UIA is higher than 0.05 mg/L, the fish are being damaged. (https://extension.rwfm.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2013/09/Ammonia-in-Aquatic-Systems1.pdf)
- The EPA says unionized ammonia is toxic because it can readily diffuse across gill membranes. It lists gill damage among the effects, but gives no 0.02 figure on that page. (https://www.epa.gov/caddis/ammonia)
- **Corrected wording:** "Long-term exposure to unionized ammonia above about 0.02 mg/L is generally considered potentially harmful to fish, including their gills. Some guides put the damage point nearer 0.05 mg/L." Sensitivity varies by species.

**Claim 3: Fresh water holds about 14.6 mg/L of oxygen at 0 °C and about 7.6 mg/L at 30 °C. Supported as written.**
- This holds for fresh water at saturation and sea-level pressure.
- The Engineers Edge table lists 14.60 mg/L at 0 °C and 7.54 mg/L at 30 °C for fresh water. (https://www.engineersedge.com/calculators/oxygen_dissolved_in_water_16058.htm) AquaText gives the same pair: 14.6 and 7.54. (https://www.aquatext.com/tables/oxygen.htm)
- An Oxford University Press table lists S = 14.62 mg/L at 0 °C and 7.56 mg/L at 30 °C. (https://global.oup.com/us/companion.websites/fdscontent/uscompanion/us/static/companion.websites/9780197651896/Table_18.2_Factors_affecting_O2_solubility.pdf)
- The British Columbia government's dissolved-oxygen guideline cites freshwater solubilities of 14.6 mg/L at 0 °C. (https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/air-land-water/water/waterquality/water-quality-guidelines/approved-wqgs/dissolvedoxygen-tech.pdf)
- The tables give 7.54–7.56 at 30 °C, which rounds to 7.5 or 7.6. "About 7.6" is acceptable. Adding "at sea-level pressure, at saturation" would make the claim more precise.
